new_statements.quote: Fíjese en que el estrés secundario, en muchos casos, corresponde a una vocal larga (hablando fonéticamente). Parece que la duración silábica era el factor principal para Tessmann en sus indicaciones de estrés (indicado por un acento agudo). Sin embargo, mis datos preliminares sugieren que los correlatos principales del estrés primario son el tono y la intensidad. [2022 slides, p.111:] Approximately 40 nouns, mostly fauna terms – Most end in high tone in isolation (cf. Urarina) – Evidence for H-L lexical tone contrasts from nouns without final H
new_statements.translation: Note that secondary stress, in many cases, corresponds to a long vowel (phonetically speaking). It seems that syllable duration was the main factor for Tessmann in his indications of stress (marked with an acute accent). However, my preliminary data suggest that the principal correlates of primary stress are pitch (tone) and intensity.
new_statements.citation: O'Hagan, Zachary J. 2011. Informe de campo del idioma omurano. Ms., University of California, Berkeley (Cabeceras Aid Project), 22 Sept 2011; supplemented by O'Hagan 2022 Fieldwork Forum slides (UC Berkeley, 2 Nov 2022).

Sin embargo, mis datos preliminares sugieren que los correlatos principales del estres primario son el tono y la intensidad.') are present verbatim (extracted text). new_statements.rule_in_words: No positional stress rule is stated anywhere. In 2011 O'Hagan transcribes a primary stress (acute) whose correlates are pitch and intensity and a secondary stress (grave) tied to phonetic vowel length; in his 20-item table the primary stress is word-final in 14 of 20 items, penultimate in 5, initial in 1 (my count). By 2022/2023 he reanalyses this prominence as tone: most nouns end in a high tone in isolation (as in neighbouring Urarina), with a lexical H-L contrast shown by a few nouns lacking final H (pápà 'father'); the 2023 chapter (p. 951 snippet) notes Tessmann's 1920s accent marks frequently sit on different syllables from the modern high tone.
new_statements.secondary_stress: 2011: 'secondary stress' (grave accent) said to correspond in many cases to a phonetically long vowel, typically on the first syllable (e.g. ò:pí, lù:né, mà:má).
new_statements.exceptions: Non-final primary stress in tSà:tánI 'hombre', napítSu 'pava', tà:tánə 'paujil', maRátSi 'perro', natSúRi 'wiracocha', túnitSa 'remo' (2011 table); 2023: pápà 'father' the only disyllable with the H-L pattern (snippet).
new_statements.domain_note: All data are citation forms of c. 20-40 isolated nouns elicited from rememberers/semi-speakers (José Manuel Macusi Nuribe 2011; Juan and Jorge Macusi Nuribe 2013); 'in isolation' explicitly. No phrase-level data. Language functionally extinct; analysis necessarily preliminary.
new_statements.identity_note: Omurano proper (omur1241; a.k.a. Humurana/Roamaina/Mayna, not to be confused with Maynas), as remembered by Urarina-dominant semi-speakers of the Macusi family on the lower/middle Urituyacu in 2011-2013; c. 20-40 nouns in isolation. Glottolog's second 'phonology' ref for this languoid (Zehetner 1978, Die Mundart der Hallertau) is a Bavarian German dialect monograph mis-attached to omur1241 and irrelevant.

Urarina) – Evidence for H-L lexical tone contrasts from nouns without final H'. I.e. word prominence reanalysed as tone, predominantly word-final H; no use of the word 'stress'.
